blocks.text: Build Your Job Search Foundation

Most people start a job search the same way: update an old CV and start scrolling job boards. A few applications later, things already feel chaotic and unfocused. But there's a better way to begin.

Throughout this guide, you'll build a complete, AI-supported job search system: from identifying your strengths and choosing target roles to applying effectively, preparing for interviews, and negotiating offers.
The Job Search Workflow
Before you touch a single application, you need to answer these questions:

• What can I do?
  • Where do those skills fit?
  • What direction am I targeting?
That's the workflow you'll follow in this lesson — extract your skills, research the market, identify your direction, and write a positioning statement that ties it all together.
Every piece of your job search — your CV, cover letter, LinkedIn profile, outreach messages — should tell the same consistent story. That story starts here.
Meet Dip Singh and Gabi
You'll practice alongside two professionals throughout this course.

• Dip Singh has spent 8 years in digital marketing — SEO, paid acquisition, and team management at B2B companies. He's looking for his next role in the same field.
  • Gabi is a mechanical engineer with 6 years of experience who's ready to transition into project management.
Two different starting points, one shared goal: a focused, AI-supported job search. You'll see how the same techniques work for both.

Whether you're staying in your field like Dip Singh or making a career shift like Gabi, the first step is the same: get clear on what you bring to the table. Not what your job title says, but what you've done, built, solved, and learned. That's where a skills inventory comes in.
What Is a Skills Inventory?

A skills inventory is a structured overview of your skills and tangible results: hard skills, soft skills, transferable strengths, and measurable achievements. This is the raw material behind your entire job search — the foundation for your CV, your positioning, and every application you'll write.

feedbackCorrect.text: A skills inventory goes deeper than job titles or personality descriptors. It captures what you did, how well you did it, and which strengths transfer across roles — backed by specific tools, methods, numbers, or outcomes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Job titles show positions, not capabilities. And general personality traits like "hardworking" sound positive, but don't tell employers anything specific. A strong inventory focuses on concrete skills, quantifiable results, and transferable strengths — tied to real experience, not self-descriptions.

options.label: A list of job titles held in chronological order
Technical skills tied to specific tools or methods
Measurable achievements from past roles
General personality traits like "hardworking" or "detail-oriented”
Transferable skills from non-work experience

blocks.question: What should a strong skills inventory include?

blocks.text: Most people undercount their skills. They forget what they picked up across projects, side responsibilities, and cross-functional work. AI can help surface patterns you might overlook — but only if you give it enough real context to work with. A vague input gets a vague inventory.
Extract Your Skills with AI

Claude is a strong choice for skills extraction. It handles long, unstructured input well and identifies patterns across roles, projects, and non-traditional experience, which makes it useful when your career path isn't a straight line. Let's practice with Dip Singh, a marketing professional with 8 years of experience who's searching for his next role in the same field.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Hard skills: project management, data analysis, communication, budgeting, content creation.

Soft skills: leadership, teamwork, problem-solving, adaptability, time management, critical thinking.
blocks.prompt: Help Dip Singh start building his skills inventory with Claude.
blocks.template: I want to find a new job. Identify my [skill types] that I should highlight to employers

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly. Claude returned a generic checklist because Dip Singh didn't provide any details about his actual work. Without specifics — roles, responsibilities, results — any AI will default to broad, obvious answers that could apply to anyone.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The real issue is missing context. Claude had no information about Dip Singh's actual background, so it produced a generic list. When you give AI specific experience details — roles, achievements, scope — the output becomes specific and personal too.

options.label: The list includes too many skills to be useful
The prompt gave Claude no actual experience to analyze
Hard and soft skills should be requested separately
Claude can't reliably identify professional skills

blocks.question: Dip Singh got a skills list. What's the biggest problem with this output?

blocks.exampleResponse: Hard skills: - SEO strategy (40% organic traffic growth) - Google Ads ($50K/mo budgets) - Content planning across 3 channels Soft skills: - Cross-team communication - Stakeholder reporting Transferable strengths: - Data-driven decision-making - Budget management - Campaign project management
blocks.prompt: Now give Claude specific context about Dip Singh's experience.
blocks.template: I've worked as [role] [time period] managing SEO, paid ads, and a team of 4 at B2B companies. Identify my hard skills, soft skills, and [skill type].

blocks.text: Specificity Changes Everything
See the difference? When Dip Singh shared his actual role, scope, and responsibilities, Claude returned specific, evidence-based skills instead of a generic checklist.

• Career changers: If you're shifting fields like Gabi, your inventory surfaces transferable skills you may not think to name.
  • Freelancers and contractors: If you've built your career through projects rather than traditional roles, an inventory helps you translate scattered experience into a coherent professional story.
  • Returning professionals: If you've taken time away — for caregiving, a break, or personal reasons — your inventory helps you reconnect with what you built before and reframe it for today's market.

blocks.text: Research the Market With AI
The next step is understanding where your skills fit. Market research helps you identify realistic roles, see what employers actually require, and catch skill gaps before they cost you interviews.

Perplexity is a strong tool for this step. Unlike general chatbots, it draws on current web sources and provides citations, so you can trace where salary data, role requirements, or industry trends come from.
Let's conduct market research for Gabi, a mechanical engineer with 6 years' experience who is exploring a transition into project management.

blocks.exampleResponse: Top Project Management paths for engineers: - Technical Project Management ($110-$120K, Agile + stakeholder skills) - *source*, - Construction Project Management ($90-$100K, leverages engineering directly) - *source* - IT Project Manamgement ($100-$110K, PMP or Scrum cert preferred) - *source* Key skill gaps for engineers: - Formal PM methodology - Budgeting software - Cross-functional communication frameworks
blocks.prompt: Use Perplexity to help Gabi research roles that match her background.
blocks.template: What are the most in-demand [role type] for someone transitioning from [background]? Include typical salary ranges, required skills, and [additional detail].

blocks.text: Excellent!
Perplexity gave Gabi a starting point — project management paths that connect to her background, realistic salary ranges, and the gaps she'll need to close.

• Treat these figures as a starting benchmark, not a final answer. AI pulls from available web sources, which may not reflect your specific city, industry niche, or company size.
  • Cross-check on dedicated platforms like Glassdoor, LinkedIn Salary, or Levels.fyi — especially before entering any salary conversation. The more sources you compare, the more accurate your range will be.
blocks.title: Verify Before You Negotiate

blocks.text: Write Your Positioning Statement

A positioning statement is a short paragraph that connects who you are professionally, what you're strongest at, and where you're headed. It's a reference point you'll use to keep your CV, cover letter, LinkedIn, and outreach consistent throughout the job search.
Before you write any application material, your positioning statement answers one question, "What's my professional story, and how does it lead to the role I want?" Let's help Dip Singh draft his.

blocks.exampleResponse: Dip Singh is a digital marketing professional with 8 years leading SEO strategy, paid acquisition, and cross-functional campaign teams in B2B. His consistent record of measurable growth in organic traffic and advertising ROI positions him for senior roles where data-driven marketing leadership drives business outcomes.
blocks.prompt: Help Dip Singh draft a positioning statement with Claude.
blocks.template: Based on this background, *experience summary*, write a concise [document type] connecting my strengths to [role]

blocks.text: Perfect!

Dip Singh's positioning statement is specific, grounded in real experience, and directly points to his target role. He can now use it as a reference every time he writes a CV summary, a LinkedIn headline, or a cover letter opening — and stay consistent across all of them.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. This statement is pure filler — it could describe anyone in any industry. A strong positioning statement names the specific field, key strengths, and target direction. If you remove the person's name and it still sounds like it could be anyone's, it's not specific enough.

feedbackIncorrect.text: It sounds polished, but it says almost nothing. "Results-driven," "proven track record," and "dynamic environment" are generic phrases that don't tell an employer anything specific. A positioning statement needs to name your field, your strengths, and your direction.

options.label: Weak
Strong

blocks.question: "Results-driven professional with a proven track record of success seeking to leverage extensive skills and experience in a dynamic, fast-paced environment"

blocks.text:
• Positioning before applications: A strong job search starts with understanding your skills, your market, and your direction — not with updating your CV.
  • Specificity drives AI quality: The more concrete details you provide (real experience, actual numbers, specific goals), the more useful and actionable the output becomes.
  • Right tool for the right task: Claude excels at extracting patterns from unstructured experience, Perplexity delivers sourced market data you can verify, and ChatGPT is effective for comparing options and building structured plans.

Build a CV That Works

Imagine this: you spend an hour polishing your CV, hit send on 15 applications, and hear nothing back. Not because you lack experience, but because your CV reads exactly like the last 200 CVs in the pile. This lesson fixes that.

Let's get started!
CV Writing Strategy

You'll build a master CV, then learn how to adapt it for each specific position. Different roles prioritize different skills — even within the same field. A Senior Marketing Manager posting might emphasize analytics and team leadership, while a Growth Marketing role at a startup wants scrappy experimentation and speed. Your CV needs to reflect that every time.
Anatomy of a Strong CV

Before you start writing bullet points, you need to understand what goes where. A well-structured CV has a clear hierarchy: a concise professional summary at the top, followed by experience, skills, and education.
Each section earns its place by answering a specific employer question:

• Your professional summary (2-3 sentences) adapts your positioning statement for the role.

And even when it's optional, a tailored cover letter can set you apart — especially for competitive roles or career transitions where your CV alone doesn't tell the full story.
The Cover Letter Structure
A strong cover letter has three sections, staying under one page (250-400 words across 3-4 paragraphs).

• Who am I = a brief statement of your professional identity and what you do best, connected to the role.
  • Why this company = a specific reason this employer stands out, based on their mission, recent work, or strategic direction.
  • Why me = the strongest evidence from your experience that proves you can deliver what the role requires.

The body of the cover letter is where you connect specific company priorities to your actual results — not where you summarize your CV.

The intro and closing should be tight and direct. If any section feels like filler, cut it or make it more specific. Generic flattery ("I admire your innovative company culture") does more harm than good, as it signals that you didn't research the company and therefore lack motivation.
Research the Company First

Perplexity is useful here — it pulls sourced, current information about company news, mission statements, recent product launches, or strategic priorities. blocks.text: What's Next

Network Like a Professional

Many jobs are never publicly posted. They're filled through referrals, internal moves, and direct outreach. That means your applications — no matter how polished — only reach a fraction of what's available. Networking opens the rest. And LinkedIn is where most of that networking happens. This lesson shows you how to make it work.
Why Networking Matters

Networking is building professional relationships that create opportunities — referrals, introductions, insider knowledge about open roles, and advice from people who've been where you're going. It works through multiple channels: industry events, alumni groups, professional communities, and online platforms.

Of all these channels, LinkedIn is the most scalable for job seekers. It's where recruiters actively search, where hiring managers post roles, and where you can reach people at target companies without a warm introduction.
What LinkedIn Does for Your Job Search
LinkedIn serves three roles at once:

• It's a public CV that recruiters find through a search.
  • It's a networking tool for reaching people at target companies.
  • It's a content platform where you can demonstrate expertise.
Use all three functions and keep them aligned with the same career narrative you've built in your CV and cover letter.
Your Public CV

Think of LinkedIn as the public-facing version of your career narrative. It should tell the same story as your CV and cover letter — but adapted for how people browse profiles. That means your headline, About section, and top experience entries need to do the work in the first few seconds.
Start With the Headline
Your LinkedIn headline isn't your current job title — it's a short positioning statement. You get 220 characters to tell someone what you do, who you do it for, and what makes you worth clicking on.

blocks.exampleResponse:
1. Senior Digital Marketing Professional | SEO & Paid Acquisition | 40% Organic Growth for B2B
  2. B2B Marketing Lead | Data-Driven Growth | SEO, Google Ads, Team Management
  3. Digital Marketing Strategist | $50K/mo Ad Budgets | Driving Measurable B2B Growth

blocks.text: What Makes a Headline Work

Three options, each with a different emphasis — results, skills, or scope. Dip Singh can pick the one that best matches his target roles, or mix elements from all three. The key is that every headline names something specific instead of just a job title.
Write Your About Section

The About section is your chance to tell your professional story in your own voice. It should read like a short, confident introduction: who you are, what you're strongest at, and what you're looking for. Keep it to 3-5 short paragraphs. Claude handles this well because it maintains a natural tone across longer text without sounding robotic.

blocks.exampleResponse:
I've spent 6 years in mechanical engineering, not just designing products, but managing the full delivery process: timelines, budgets, cross-functional teams, and stakeholder expectations. 

Now I'm channeling that experience into Technical Project Management, where the skills I've built in engineering translate directly into leading complex projects from start to finish. I'm drawn to roles where technical depth and structured delivery intersect, and I'm actively pursuing project management positions in product-driven companies.

blocks.text: Narrative Arc Over CV Summary

Gabi's About section doesn't sound like a CV summary pasted into LinkedIn. It has a clear narrative arc — where she's been, what she's learned, and where she's going. That personal voice is what makes the About section different from other parts of your application.
Align Your Experience Section

Your LinkedIn experience entries should mirror your CV bullet points — but you don't need to copy them word for word. LinkedIn is more conversational, and you can include slightly more context than a CV allows. The key rule stays the same: outcomes over duties, evidence over descriptions.

If you've already written strong CV bullets with AI, adapting them for LinkedIn is quick. Paste your top 2-3 bullets per role, adjust the tone to be slightly less formal, and make sure the keywords match your target role.
Find the Right People to Connect With

Before you send an outreach message, you need to know who to reach out to. Use LinkedIn's search filters to find people by job title, company, and location. Look for professionals in your target role, hiring managers at companies you're interested in, and people who've made a similar career transition.

Start with 10-15 profiles. Read their About sections and recent activity. The more you know about someone before reaching out, the more specific — and effective — your message will be. A connection request to someone whose post you've read is far stronger than a blind request to a stranger with the right job title.
Write Outreach Messages That Get Responses

Networking is about writing short, specific messages that give the other person a reason to respond. The best outreach messages are 3-4 sentences: who you are, why you're reaching out to them specifically, and one clear, low-effort ask.

I came across your profile and noticed you made a similar move from engineering. I'd love to hear how you approached the transition and whether Celqo Engineering supports that kind of internal growth. Thanks for reading — happy to keep it brief!

You don't need to become a LinkedIn influencer. But 1-2 posts per month about your professional journey or an industry insight can increase your visibility to recruiters and hiring managers. It signals that you're active, thoughtful, and engaged with your field.

Short, specific, and ends with a question. Dip Singh shared a real insight from his experience — not a generic motivational quote or tip. That's the kind of post that gets engagement without feeling forced.
Build a Networking Plan

Random outreach doesn't work. A networking plan gives you structure: who to contact, how often, and through which channels.

A realistic plan for someone job-searching while employed might look like 3-5 new connections per week, 1 informational message, and 1 LinkedIn post per month. Remember that consistency matters more than volume.
Beyond LinkedIn
LinkedIn is the primary platform for most job searches, but it's not the only one. If you're in tech, a clean GitHub profile or contributions to open-source projects signal real skills.

Creative professionals benefit from Behance or Dribbble. Analysts and data professionals can showcase work through Kaggle or a personal blog. Pick one secondary platform that fits your field and keep it consistent with your LinkedIn narrative.

From Applications to Results

You can have the strongest CV, cover letter, and LinkedIn profile in the world — but if you're applying to the wrong places, through the wrong channels, with no system to track what's working, you're leaving results on the table. This lesson turns your job search into a repeatable, trackable process.
Applying Is a System

Most job seekers treat applications like a numbers game — send as many as possible and hope something sticks. That approach burns time and energy fast. An effective job search works more like a funnel: you identify the right channels, tailor each application to the role, track everything, and adjust based on what gets results.
Know Your Application Channels
There are four main channels for job applications, and each works differently:

• Job boards (LinkedIn Jobs, Indeed, Glassdoor) give you volume and filters.
  • Company career pages often have roles not posted elsewhere.
  • Recruiter outreach lets you skip the queue by going directly to hiring teams.
  • Referrals through your network have the highest conversion rate.

The strongest results come from targeted channels — referrals, direct outreach, and company career pages — where your application stands out because it's specific and intentional.

Tailor Applications With AI

You've already learned how to tailor your CV and write a personalized cover letter. Now it's about doing that efficiently across multiple applications without sacrificing quality. The goal isn't to spend an hour per application — it's to spend the right 15-20 minutes on each one.

ChatGPT handles quick tailoring well. Give it your master CV, the job description, and clear instructions, and it can suggest which bullet points to prioritize and which language to adjust. For deeper rewrites, use Claude — it's better at maintaining tone across a full document.

Speed Up Your Search Without Cutting Corners
Tailoring every application takes time. But there are three AI techniques that make the process significantly faster without sacrificing quality. They save time without cutting corners.
Score the Fit Before You Apply

Not every job posting is worth 20 minutes of tailoring. Before you invest time, paste the job description into ChatGPT or Claude, along with your master CV, and ask it to rate the fit between your experience and this role on a scale of 1-10. Research Companies in Batches

Instead of researching each company one by one before every application, batch the work. Pick 5-7 target companies at the start of the week and use Perplexity to research all of them in one sitting — mission, recent news, strategic priorities, and team culture.
Save the results in a document. When it's time to tailor a cover letter or outreach message, you already have the material ready.
Build a Prompt Library

You'll reuse the same types of prompts dozens of times — tailoring a CV summary, writing a cover letter opening, drafting a recruiter message. Save your best-performing prompts as templates with placeholders for the company name, role, and key details. Now you're not reinventing the prompt every time — just swapping in new details.
Reach Recruiters Directly

Not every application should go through a job board. For roles you're serious about, sending a short message directly to the hiring manager or recruiter on LinkedIn can put your name in front of the right person before the ATS even sees your CV. This works especially well when paired with a strong profile.

blocks.text: Follow-Up Over Cold Outreach

AI is a powerful tool for tailoring and organizing your job search. But some practices cross the line. Mass-applying with automation tools that submit hundreds of identical applications, using AI to fabricate experience, or generating entire cover letters without any personal input — these approaches are increasingly flagged by employers.

Being transparent and using AI as an assistant — not a replacement for your own thinking — keeps your applications honest and your reputation intact. The rule is straightforward: AI sharpens your real experience, it doesn't create it.

blocks.question: Is salary alone a reliable way to evaluate a job offer?

blocks.text: Evaluate Beyond Salary

A job offer is more than a number on a page — the full picture only emerges when you look at what surrounds it. Comparing offers on salary alone is like evaluating a job by its title — you might miss important information.
The Offer Evaluation Framework
Use 6 categories to compare any offer systematically.

• Compensation: base salary, bonuses, equity, and a raise timeline
  • Benefits: health insurance, retirement contributions, paid time off, parental leave
  • Role scope: responsibilities, team size, decision-making authority
  • Growth: promotion path, learning budget, mentorship, skill development
  • Work conditions: remote/hybrid/onsite, flexibility, travel requirements
  • Culture and stability: company values, team dynamics, financial health

Not every category carries equal weight — and your priorities will differ from someone else's. A parent might prioritize flexibility and benefits. An early-career professional might place greater weight on growth and learning than on base salary. Before you compare offers, you need to know what matters most to you.
Benchmark Salary with AI

Before you can negotiate, you need to know what the market pays. Gemini,Google's AI assistant, is useful for salary benchmarking because it pulls from broad web sources — Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, PayScale, and industry reports — giving you a range rather than a single number. This helps you understand where an offer falls relative to the market.

Companies with strong equity programs may offer lower base but higher total compensation.

  • Culture and stability: company values, team dynamics, financial health

Not every category carries equal weight — and your priorities will differ from someone else's. A parent might prioritize flexibility and benefits. An early-career professional might place greater weight on growth and learning than on base salary. Before you compare offers, you need to know what matters most to you.
Benchmark Salary with AI

Before you can negotiate, you need to know what the market pays. Gemini,Google's AI assistant, is useful for salary benchmarking because it pulls from broad web sources — Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, PayScale, and industry reports — giving you a range rather than a single number. This helps you understand where an offer falls relative to the market.

blocks.title: Pro Tip

blocks.text: Respond to Offers Professionally

How you respond to an offer matters as much as what you say. Even if you plan to negotiate, your first response should be positive and appreciative. Acknowledge the offer, express genuine interest, and ask for time to review. Most employers expect this and will give you 3-5 business days.

blocks.text: Acknowledgment Before Negotiation

Warm, professional, and buys Dip Singh time to prepare for his negotiation. He didn't accept immediately, and didn't start negotiating in the same email. Separating acknowledgment from negotiation gives you space to prepare properly.

Now that Dip Singh has bought himself time, the next step is to prepare for the negotiation itself. And how you make your case matters as much as what you ask for.

feedbackCorrect.text: Evidence-based negotiation works because it gives the employer a reason to say yes. Your results show what you've delivered, and market data shows what the role is worth. Together, they make the case without pressure or ultimatums.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Competing offers and aggressive anchoring can backfire — they shift the tone from collaboration to pressure. The most effective negotiations present concrete evidence (your results and market data) that makes a higher number feel justified, not demanded.

blocks.question: What makes a salary negotiation most effective?

blocks.text: Negotiate With Evidence, Not Pressure
Negotiation is about presenting evidence for why a different number or condition is reasonable. The strongest negotiations reference market data or the specific value you bring.

Claude is particularly useful here because negotiation language requires precision and tone control. A message that's too casual can seem unprofessional. One that's too formal can feel cold. Claude handles that balance well — direct but respectful.

Subject: Re: Senior Marketing Manager offer — compensation discussion

Hi *Name*, 

Thank you again for the offer — I'm excited about the role and the team. After reviewing the full package and researching market benchmarks for this level, I'd like to discuss the base salary. 

Given my 8 years of experience driving measurable results — including 40% organic traffic growth and 25% cost-per-lead reduction — I believe a base in the $120-125K range would better reflect the value I'd bring to Velmix. I'm flexible and happy to discuss this further. 

Looking forward to finding the right fit for both sides.

Best,
Dip Singh

blocks.text: Evidence Over Pressure
Dip Singh's email is specific, data-backed, and collaborative. He named a range (not a single number), referenced his results, and left the door open for discussion.
Negotiate Beyond Salary

If the employer can't move on salary, there's often flexibility on other terms. Extra PTO days, remote work arrangements, a signing bonus, professional development budget, or a shorter review cycle for a raise — these are all negotiable and can significantly improve an offer's total value.
Handle Rejections and Declines Gracefully

Not every negotiation ends with a yes. And not every offer is the right one to accept. How you decline — or respond to a rejection of your counteroffer — matters for your professional reputation. A gracious decline keeps the relationship alive for future opportunities.

blocks.text: Decline Without Closing Doors

Gabi declined without burning a bridge. She was specific about her reason, expressed genuine gratitude, and left the door open. That last line isn't just politeness — industries are smaller than you think, and the same recruiter may have a better-fit role 6 months from now.

• Evaluate the full picture: Use the six-category framework — compensation, benefits, role scope, growth, work conditions, and culture — to compare offers beyond salary alone.
  • Benchmark before you negotiate: Gemini and Perplexity give you market data, so your ask is grounded in evidence, not guesswork.
  • Negotiate with evidence, not pressure: Specific results and market data make the case for you. Collaborative tone gets better outcomes than ultimatums.
  • Every response shapes your reputation: Whether you accept, counter, or decline — be professional, specific, and gracious.
